name: Argon laser whitening

lead:
Argon laser whitening is a professional teeth-whitening method in which a peroxide gel is applied to the teeth and a dental laser or curing light is used to energize it. The aim is a visibly lighter shade of the smile in one appointment.
A whiter smile is one of the most noticed features of a face, so in-office whitening is a popular cosmetic step. Dental literature on light activation overall reports mixed findings on whether the light adds anything beyond the peroxide itself.

paras: A dentist protects the gums, applies a high-concentration peroxide gel and exposes it to light for a set time, sometimes in more than one round. Results are measured against a shade guide. Whitening fades over time, so touch-ups are common.

In-office peroxide whitening commonly causes tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, and heat from light sources is a recognized concern. Reported sensitivity in studies of in-office peroxide-and-heat treatments ranged from 67 to 78 percent of patients. A dentist assesses suitability, for example for restorations or sensitive teeth.

chain: Laser or light energizes the gel
Stains break down, teeth look whiter
angle.text: The whitening comes from the peroxide, which breaks down pigment molecules in the teeth; the laser is used to accelerate it in a single sitting. The result is a lighter smile that lasts until stains build up again.

lead: Argon laser whitening refers to in-office tooth bleaching in which a laser, historically an argon dental laser, is used to light-activate a peroxide whitening gel. It belongs to the broader family of light-accelerated whitening that also uses halogen, LED and plasma arc lamps [1].

The appearance payoff is a lighter tooth shade; in-office bleaching can improve shade by roughly two to seven levels, sometimes over more than one visit [1]. Light is thought to speed peroxide breakdown, with blue wavelengths described as most effective for activation [1].

Research on light activation in general is mixed: a 2012 meta-analysis reported that light can increase whitening when used properly, while a 2015 study found no improvement and noted possible heating of tissue [1]. No trial specific to argon lasers exists.
infobox: Light exposure of about 6-15 minutes per round

paras: In-office whitening starts with cleaning and gum protection, followed by hydrogen or carbamide peroxide gel. Peroxide releases free radicals that break down pigment molecules in the teeth [1]. Light-activated systems expose the gel to light for roughly 6 to 15 minutes per application [1].

Reviews of light activation report mixed results. A 2012 meta-analysis found extra whitening when light was used properly, whereas a 2015 study reported no improvement and possible tissue heating [1].

Between 67 and 78 percent of in-office patients reported sensitivity in studies using peroxide and heat, lasting about 4 to 39 days [1]. Peroxide free radicals may also irritate gums and affect enamel [1]. In the EU, over-the-counter products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6 percent permitted under professional supervision [1].
No studies found specific to argon laser whitening. Studies of light-activated whitening in general are summarized above.
